o: We need the shortest contiguous substring of `s1` that contains `s2` **as a subsequence** (characters in order, not necessarily adjacent), preferring the left-most one on ties. In Example 1, scanning `s1 = "abcdebdde"`, the window `"bcde"` (indices 1–4) contains `b→d→e` in order and beats the later same-length window `"bdde"`. In Example 2, `'u'` never appears in `s1`, so no window exists and we return `""`. Constraints (`|s1| ≤ 2·10⁴`, `|s2| ≤ 100`) allow an $O(n \cdot m)$ dynamic-programming solution (~2·10⁶ states) comfortably, while a naive check of every substring would be far too slow.
k: Track, for each position in s1, the earliest start index in s1 from which s2's prefix can be matched as a subsequence ending there.
A window ending at index i with start dp[i][m-1] is a candidate answer whenever s2 is fully matched.
The two-pointer forward/backward trick avoids an m-sized table by re-scanning backwards after each full match.

a.n: Approach 1: Dynamic Programming on Start Indices
a.i: Let `dp[i][j]` be the smallest starting index `k` in `s1` such that `s1[k..i]` contains `s2[0..j]` as a subsequence ending exactly at `i`. If `s1[i] == s2[j]`, this character extends a match of the previous prefix, so `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`; otherwise the match state carries over unchanged: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]`. Whenever `j == m-1` and the cell is valid, the window `s1[dp[i][m-1] .. i]` is a candidate; keep the shortest (left-most on ties). This works because each DP cell encodes the best possible left endpoint for a subsequence match ending at that exact pair of positions.
s: Initialize dp with -1 (impossible); set dp[i][0] = i when s1[i] == s2[0].
For each i from 1..n-1 and j from 1..m-1: if s1[i]==s2[j], dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1], else dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j].
Also propagate dp[i][0] = dp[i-1][0] when characters don't match.
Whenever j==m-1 and dp[i][j] != -1, compare window length i-dp[i][j]+1 against the best so far.
Return the best window, or "" if none was found.
a.t: O(n·m) time — each of the n positions updates an m-sized row once.
a.sp: O(m) space — only the previous DP row is kept.

a.i: Scan `s1` left to right trying to match `s2` as a subsequence using pointer `j`. When `j` reaches `m`, a valid window ends at the current index; now walk a second pointer backward through `s1` re-matching `s2` from its last character to its first, which finds the smallest possible left endpoint for that particular right endpoint. Record the window if it improves the answer, then reset `j` to continue searching for later windows. Each character participates in at most a constant number of pointer moves per phase, giving linear-ish behavior in practice.
s: Set j = 0; iterate i over s1, incrementing j whenever s1[i] == s2[j].
When j == m, record end = i and walk k = i backward with t = m-1, decrementing t whenever s1[k] == s2[t].
When t < 0, the window is s1[k+1 .. end]; update the answer if it is shorter.
Reset j = 0 and continue scanning from i = end + 1.
Return the recorded best window or "".
a.t: O(n·m) worst case (backward rescans can overlap), but typically near O(n) since each forward pass advances i monotonically.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the output.

w: In an interview, lead with the DP formulation since it is easy to prove correct, then mention the two-pointer method as a space-optimal refinement. Common pitfalls: confusing subsequence with substring (a sliding window with character counts does **not** work here because order matters); forgetting ties must resolve to the left-most window (use strict `<` when updating the best); mishandling the no-match case by returning `""`. Edge cases: `s2` of length 1, `s2` equal to all of `s1`, repeated characters causing many candidate windows. Follow-ups may ask for all minimum windows, or the generalization where `s2` must appear as a substring instead (that variant reduces to standard minimum window substring).
